questions.question_text: The Doppleganger phenomenon is best described as a/an
questions.explanation: It refers to the awareness of another human being accompanying the self. Reported in psychosis and in severe sleep deprivation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is she likely displaying?
questions.explanation:
A mannerism is the abnormal and occasionally bizarre performance of a voluntary, goal-directed activity (e.g. a conspicuously dramatic manner of walking). Unusual, repeated performances of a goal-directed motor action or the maintenance of an unusual modification of an adaptive posture are considered mannerisms. Examples of this sign are unusual hand movements while shaking hands, when greeting others, and during writing. Other examples may include peculiarities of dress, of hairstyle, and writing.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 114.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 90.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a formal thought disturbance?
questions.explanation:
Nancy Andreasen created a scale in which the classic formal thought disorders are subdivided into three groups:
- Communication disturbances: when the speaker does not meet the necessary requirements for the listener’s understanding (poverty of content of speech, pressure of speech, distractible speech, tangentiality, derailment, stilted speech, echolalia, self-reference, circumstantiality, loss of goal, perseveration, and blocking)
- Language disturbances: when the speaker violates the semantic and syntactic conventions (incoherence, clang association, neologisms, use of word approximations)
- Thought disturbances: when only thinking alone seems affected (poverty of thought and illogically aberrant inferential processes)
Andreasen demonstrated that these psychopathological findings were not specific to schizophrenia and were also common in other mental disorders (e.g. mania).
Ref: Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572.

questions.question_text: What is the term used to denote this type of pathological change in mood?
questions.explanation:
Anhedonia is the feeling of absent or significantly diminished enjoyment of previously pleasurable activities. It is a core symptom of depressive illness and is also a negative symptom of schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 102.

questions.question_text: What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Cotard syndrome is a presentation of psychotic depressive illness seen particularly in elderly people. There is a combination of severely depressed mood with nihilistic delusions and/or hypochondriacal delusions. The patient may state that they are already dead and should be buried, that their insides have stopped working and are rotting away, or that they have stopped existing altogether.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 105.

questions.question_text: Apathy is characterised by
questions.explanation:
Apathy is a dulled emotional tone associated with detachment or indifference.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1136.

questions.question_text: Suggestibility is a prominent feature of
questions.explanation: The role of suggestibility is important in those who present with confabulation, pseudologia, retrospective falsification or false memory. Suggestible subjects accept statements from others, act upon their commands and deny evidence from the senses or from rational understanding that would contradict these statements.

questions.question_text: This is best described as
questions.explanation:
Audible thoughts are a form of auditory hallucination in which everything the patient thinks or speaks is repeated by the voices. It is also called thought echoing.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1136.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about the psychopathology exhibited by the patient?

options.text: It is seen only in prison populations
It is not seen in schizophrenia
It is a disturbance of thought control
It is a disturbance of thought form

correct_answer.text: It is a disturbance of thought form

Ganser syndrome is a disturbance of thought form characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. It is recognised to occur in a variety of psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, dissociative disorder, malingering, organic states, etc. In ICD-11, Ganser syndrome is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul

Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.

questions.explanation: Stilted speech - speech that is excessively stilted and formal. (e.g. 'The attorney comported himself indecorously'.)

questions.question_text: Choose one incorrect statement about fugue states:

options.text: It is a dissociative reaction to unbearable stress
Fugue state generally has an insidious onset
Spontaneous resolution is a common outcome

correct_answer.text: Fugue state generally has an insidious onset

correct_answers.text: Fugue state generally has an insidious onset

questions.explanation:
Fugue is a dissociative reaction to unbearable stress. Following a severe external stressor, the affected individual develops sudden amnesia and may wander to a distant location. The amnesia will be for personal identity such as name, address, and history as well as for personal events, while at the same time the ability to perform complex behaviours is maintained. Consciousness is unimpaired. Recovery can be expected in time. Following resolution, there is amnesia for the events which occurred during the fugue.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 111, 869.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. pp. 64-65.

questions.question_text: In which of the following forms does morbid jealousy NOT usually occur?
questions.explanation:
Morbid jealousy (‘delusional jealousy’) is a delusional belief that one’s partner is being unfaithful. This can occur as part of a wider psychotic illness, secondary to organic brain damage, associated with alcohol dependence, or as a monosymptomatic delusional disorder (‘Othello syndrome’). It is not a misidentification syndrome.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 106.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions the stimulus is perceived as corresponding object but the quality of the percept is altered?
questions.explanation: Distortions are changes in perception resulting from a change in the intensity and quality of the stimulus or the spatial form of the perception.

questions.question_text: Erotomania has been reported in association with all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: DeClerambault's syndrome is a form of delusion of love (erotomania). The patient is usually a woman who believes that a celebrity / someone at a higher social status is in love with her.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following phenomena can be described as ego-syntonic?
questions.explanation:
An experience is described as ego-syntonic if it is consistent with the goals and needs of the ego and/or consistent with the individual’s ideal self-image; the reverse is the case for ego-dystonicity. In general, delusions are ego-syntonic, though as an individual with psychosis develops insight into their symptoms, delusions may seem increasingly ego-dystonic and distressing to them.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 47.

questions.question_text: The acts of praying are best termed as
questions.explanation:
A compulsion is a behaviour or action that is recognised by the patient as unnecessary and purposeless, but that they cannot resist performing repeatedly. The drive to perform the action is recognised by the patient as their own, but it is associated with a subjective sense of need to perform the act, often in order to avoid the occurrence of an adverse event.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: What is the term used to denote this type of pathological change in affect?
questions.explanation:
Incongruity of affect refers to the objective impression that the displayed affect is not consistent with the current thoughts or actions (e.g. laughing while discussing traumatic experiences). It can occur in schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 113.

options.text: Paroxysmal spike activity in premotor area
Failure to predict sensory feedback of one's own movements
Inability to control execution of motor maps

correct_answer.text: Failure to predict sensory feedback of one's own movements

correct_answers.text: Failure to predict sensory feedback of one's own movements

questions.explanation: According to this sensory-feedback model if something seems to be going wrong with the action, it is quite possible to correct for it on the basis of concurrent self-awareness. Delusions of motor control are thought to be caused by a failure to predict sensory feedback of own movements (One of the models used to explain delusions of control in patients with schizophrenia) [Ref: Gallagher, S. Psychopathology 2004; 37:8-19]

questions.question_text: This is best described as
questions.explanation:
‘Running commentary’ is a type of third-person auditory hallucination that is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia. The patient hears one or more voices providing a narrative of their current actions.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 117.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to the mental state of ecstasy?

options.text: Cannot occur in the absence of pathological phenomenon
Associated with altered boundary of self
Some degree of altered consciousness is always seen

correct_answer.text: Associated with altered boundary of self

correct_answers.text: Associated with altered boundary of self

questions.explanation:
Ecstasy is a state of extreme wellbeing associated with a feeling of rapture, bliss, and grace. It can occur in the healthy population at times of profound religious experience or occasions of deep emotion such as following childbirth. The mind is usually occupied with a feeling of communion with God or some religious figure. There may be a feeling of being in tune with the whole of nature and at one with the universe. The person in ecstasy experiences the change in ego boundaries as voluntary.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 79.

questions.question_text: Changes in the shape of objects especially with a loss of symmetry is called
questions.explanation:
Dysmegalopsia refers to a change in the perceived shape of an object. Some authors reserve the terms ‘dysmegalopsia’ to describe objects that are perceived to be larger (or smaller) on one side than the other, while others use the term generically to describe any change in perceived size. Yet others use the term ‘metamorphosia’ rather than dysmegalopsia to describe objects that are irregular in shape.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 25.

questions.question_text: Concrete thinking is usually tested by means of
questions.explanation:
Concrete thinking is characterised by the inability to understand abstract concepts and metaphorical ideas, leading to a strictly literal form of speech and the inability to comprehend allusive language (as present in proverbs). Concrete thinking can be seen in schizophrenia and dementing illnesses.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: The most likely symptom exhibited here is
questions.explanation:
Perseveration is characterised by continuing with a verbal response or action that was initially appropriate after it ceases to be apposite. It is associated with organic brain disease and is occasionally seen in schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 115.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to primary delusions?

options.text: They are more common in chronic rather than in acute schizophrenia
The content is usually aligned to cultural and social norms
Their origin can be traced back to a person's premorbid mental state
By definition, they are not understandable

correct_answer.text: By definition, they are not understandable

correct_answers.text: By definition, they are not understandable

questions.explanation:
Primary delusions are the direct result of psychopathology, while secondary delusions can be understood as having arisen in response to other primary psychiatric conditions. Jaspers maintained that primary delusions were typical of un-understandable phenomena, being immediately experienced by the patients as absolutely self-evident like an intuition or a revelation and accompanied by abnormalities in the form such as radical transformation or emergence of thinking. He designated primary delusions as delusion proper, from which secondary delusions evolve via conscious thought processes.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 106.
Hayashi N et al. Delusion progression process from the perspective of patients with psychoses: A descriptive study based on the primary delusion concept of Karl Jaspers. Plos one. 2021 Apr 27;16(4):e0250766.

questions.question_text: Vorbeireden is seen in
questions.explanation:
Vorbeireden (also known as ‘vorbeigehen’ or ‘talking past the point’) is seen in Ganser syndrome. It refers to the production of ‘approximate answers’ in which the content of the patient’s replies to questions shows that they understand what has been asked but have responded by talking about an associated topic. Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 119, 236.
Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1- 22.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 57.

questions.question_text: Deja vu and jamais vu are experiences of
questions.explanation:
Déjà vu is a sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before. Jamais vu is the sensation that events or situations are unfamiliar, although they have been experienced before. Both déjà vu and jamais vu can be everyday experiences, but also non-specific symptoms of a number of disorders, including temporal lobe epilepsy, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders. They are best described as states involving familiarity.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 105, 113.

questions.question_text: Kinaesthetic hallucination is reported in cases with
questions.explanation: Symptoms of benzodiazepine withdrawal include autonomic hyperactivity, increased tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation. anxiety (most prominent), with grand mal seizures and kinaesthetic hallucinations reported in a few patients. Excerpt from Alcohol-Related Problems: Recognition and Intervention, http://www.aafp.org/afp/1999/0115/p361.html (accessed April 11, 2015).

questions.question_text: In most cases of dysmorphophobia, the affected mental state is associated with
questions.explanation: Most cases of dysmorphophobia is associated with a major mood disorder. Most patients with Dysmorphophobia have other associated conditions like mood disorder, anxiety disorder and psychosis.

questions.question_text: To be called as age disorientation, the difference in stated age and actual age must be at least
questions.explanation:
Age disorientation is defined as misstating one’s age by 5 or more years. It was initially described as ‘perceptual distortion of temporal orientation’ in early literature. The majority of age disoriented patients underreport their age (i.e. time stood still), with a small percentage overestimating their age.
Ref: Zhand N et al. Incidental finding of age and time disorientation in a clinical sample of patients with schizophrenia: Findings from a short term follow up survey regarding cannabis use. Psychiatry Research. 2020 Aug 1;290:113150.

A mannerism is the abnormal and occasionally bizarre performance of a voluntary, goal-directed activity (e.g. a conspicuously dramatic manner of walking).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 114.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is not true with regard to depersonalisation?

options.text: Depersonalisation is rare in psychiatric practice
Depersonalisation is often a difficult experience to describe
Depersonalisation is a common experience of normal healthy people
Depersonalisation is often accompanied by the symptom of derealization
Affect is invariably involved in depersonalisation

correct_answer.text: Depersonalisation is rare in psychiatric practice

correct_answers.text: Depersonalisation is rare in psychiatric practice

questions.explanation:
Depersonalisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if they have become ‘unreal’. It is a feeling that one is not oneself or that something has changed. Depersonalisation is a non-specific symptom occurring in many psychiatric disorders, as well as in ‘normal’ people.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 108.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10.

questions.question_text: The form of psychopathology exhibited here is
questions.explanation:
An obsession is an idea, image, or impulse that is recognised by the patient as their own, but which is experienced as repetitive, intrusive, and distressing. The return of the obsession can be resisted for a time, at the expense of mounting anxiety. In some situations, the anxiety accompanying the obsessional thoughts can be relieved by associated compulsions.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 115.

questions.question_text: A sense of perplexity and uncertainty that exists during a prodrome of psychosis may be linked most appropriately to which of the following experiences?
questions.explanation:
Delusional mood is recalled as arising following a period when there is an abnormal mood state characterised by anticipatory anxiety, a sense of ‘something is about to happen’ and an increased sense of the significance of minor events. The development of the formed delusion may come as a relief to the patient in this situation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: Epileptic automatism is associated with

options.text: Duration lasting few seconds to few minutes

correct_answer.text: Duration lasting few seconds to few minutes

correct_answers.text: Duration lasting few seconds to few minutes

questions.explanation:
An automatism is a behaviour which is apparently conscious in nature, occurring in the absence of full consciousness (e.g. during a temporal lobe seizure). They typically last for several seconds to minutes. Common automatisms include oral automatisms (repetitive licking or smacking of the lips, swallowing, or kissing) and manual automatisms (fumbling with clothing, scratching, rubbing the abdomen, or fidgeting). Other physical manifestations are simple actions such as standing, walking, pacing, or even driving.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 103.
Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 214.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics
The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature.
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds, or voices that may be characteristically malign and threatening

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics

correct_answers.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics

questions.explanation:
Alcoholic hallucinosis is a substance-induced psychotic illness that is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. InICD-11, it is designated as “alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations”. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings). With continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. Unlike delirium tremens, those with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking. In 5%, symptoms persist with abstinence. Persisting symptoms may be treated with antipsychotics.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 602.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes the above?
questions.explanation:
Thought insertion is the delusional belief that thoughts are being placed in the patient’s head from the outside. Thought insertion is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 118.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation:
Carl Schneider claimed that five features of formal thought disorders could be identified:
- Derailment: the thought slides on to a subsidiary thought
- Substitution: a major thought is substituted by a subsidiary one
- Omission: senseless omission of a thought or part of it
- Fusion: heterogenous elements of thought are interwoven with each other
- Drivelling: a disordered intermixture of constituent parts of one complex thought
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 55.

questions.question_text: What symptom is she exhibiting?
questions.explanation:
Fregoli syndrome is a type of delusional misidentification in which the patient believes that strangers have been replaced with familiar people. It may be believed that various people whom the subject meets are really the same person, in disguise. For example, a patient believed that her neighbour could change his appearance, clothes, and even his sex at will so as to spy on her.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 111.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 127.

questions.question_text: This is best described as a
questions.explanation:
A pseudo-hallucination is a false perception that is perceived as occurring as part of one’s internal experience, not as part of the external world. It may be described as having an ‘as if’ quality or as being seen with the mind’s eye. Pseudo-hallucinations are a type of mental image that, although clear and vivid, lack the substantiality of perceptions. Pseudo-hallucinations are seen in full consciousness, known to be not real perceptions, and are located not in objective space but in subjective space (for example, inside the head). Like true hallucinations, they are involuntary. Pseudo-hallucinations can occur in all modalities of sensation and are described in psychotic, organic, and drug-induced conditions, as well as occasionally in ‘normal’ individuals. (The hallucinations of deceased spouses commonly described by widows and widowers may have a form of a pseudo-hallucination.)
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 116.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 28.

questions.question_text: Phantom mirror image is a synonymous term for which one of the following hallucinations?
questions.explanation:
Autoscopy (also known as ‘phantom mirror image’) is the experience of seeing a visual hallucination or pseudo-hallucination of oneself. It is not just a visual hallucination because kinaesthetic and somatic sensation must also be present to give the subject the impression that the hallucination is oneself.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 103.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019.p. 36.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation:
A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation:
Capgras syndrome is a type of delusional misidentification in which the patient believes that a person known to them has been replaced by a ‘double’ who is to all external appearances identical, but is not the ‘real person’. This syndrome can occur both in psychiatric disorders, mainly psychotic disorders (especially schizophrenia) as well as major affective disorders, and neurocognitive disorders (e.g., post-traumatic encephalopathy, epilepsy, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, and delirium/acute confusional state).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.
Karakasi MV et al. In fear of the most loved ones. A comprehensive review on Capgras misidentification phenomenon and case report involving attempted murder under Capgras syndrome in a relapse of a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Journal of forensic and legal medicine. 2019 Aug 1;66:8-24.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not included in the classification of Delusional Disorders in ICD 10?
questions.explanation: Delusions of control are bizarre delusions seen often in schizophrenia-like disorders, and not in a persistent delusional disorder.

questions.question_text: Pseudologia fantastica is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation: Pseudologia fantastica or fluent plausible lying (pathological lying) is seen in personality disorders of antisocial or hysterical type. It often carries a grandiose tinge and can be triggered by a personal crisis, such as facing legal proceedings. A person with pseudologia may believe their own stories and often there is a blur between fantasy and reality. When confronted, these individuals may admit to lying.

questions.question_text: Dereistic thinking is a term used to describe which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Dereism is mental activity that follows a totally subjective and idiosyncratic system of logic. It is undirected fantasy thinking that fails to take the facts of reality or experience into consideration.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1138.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 43.

Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul

questions.question_text: Agitated depression is a well-recognized feature of
questions.explanation:
Agitated depression is a combination of depressed mood and psychomotor agitation, contrasting with the more usual association of depressed mood with psychomotor retardation. It is a common presentation of depression in the elderly.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 102.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning the psychopathology of morbid jealousy?

options.text: It is not seen as an isolated phenomenon
The belief can be held with delusional fixity
It is more common in women than men
It intensifies on geographical separation of partners

correct_answer.text: The belief can be held with delusional fixity

correct_answers.text: The belief can be held with delusional fixity

questions.explanation:
Morbid jealousy (‘delusional jealousy’) is a fixed delusional belief that one’s partner is being unfaithful. This can occur as part of a wider psychotic illness, secondary to organic brain damage, associated with alcohol dependence, or as a monosymptomatic delusional disorder (‘Othello syndrome’). It is more common in men. Apart from delusions of infidelity, these patients tend not to show any other symptoms. Separation from the focus of delusional ideas is advised, as behaviour may progress to violence against the partner and even to murder.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 106, 230-234.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 51.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a core feature of Ganser syndrome?

options.text: Approximate answers or VORBEIGEHEN (to pass by)

questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome refers to the production of approximate answers. e.g. Question: "What is the capital of France?" - Answer: "London". It is occasionally associated with organic brain illness but is much more commonly seen as a form of malingering in those attempting to feign mental illness e.g. in prisoners awaiting trial.

questions.question_text: The term anhedonia was coined by
questions.explanation:
Anhedonia is an inability to enjoy anything in life or even get pleasure from everyday events (for example, being hugged by one’ children or waking up to a fine spring morning). ‘Anhedonia’ was coined by Ribot, a French psychologist, in 1896.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 77.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation:
Logoclonia refers to meaningless repetition of a syllable, especially an end syllable of a word. Palilalia and stuttering have disorders that are similar to those of logoclonia. Palilalia, however, refers to the repetition of an entire word, but not a syllable. Stuttering is the involuntary disruption or blocking of speech with sound repetition, especially the initial consonants of a word, and, unlike logoclonia, stuttering is accompanied by tense and effortful utterance.
Ref: Nakagawa Y et al. Logoclonia might be a Characteristic of Logopenic Variant Primary Progressive Aphasia at an Advanced Stage: Potential Mechanisms Underlying Logoclonia. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2019 Jan 1;70(2):515-24.

questions.question_text: Common characteristics of schizophrenic auditory hallucinations include all except
questions.explanation:
Auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia are often experienced as voices although they can also take the form of other non-verbal sounds. Many such voices can be reported by patients as being similar or just like hearing other people speak. Voice-hearers report on average 3 different voices. Voices may be male or female; however, male voices are more common than female voices. Hallucinated voices frequently speak with accents different to the region or social class of the patient. There is considerable variability in the frequency of auditory hallucinations in people with schizophrenia, typically ranging from once or twice weekly to continuous.
Ref: Larøi F et al. The characteristic features of auditory verbal hallucinations in clinical and nonclinical groups: state-of-the-art overview and future directions. Schizophrenia bulletin. 2012 Jul 1;38(4):724-33.

questions.question_text: What is the term for this?
questions.explanation:
The type-token ratio is a measure for lexical diversity. It is a ratio of the number of words used in the sample (# of types): all words in the sample (# of tokens).
Ref: de Boer JN et al. Language disturbances in schizophrenia: the relation with antipsychotic medication. NPJ schizophrenia. 2020 Sep 7;6(1):1-9.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a mixed affective state?
questions.explanation: In mixed states incongruity between motor features and mood state is found: mania with inhibition, depression with excitation etc.

It can occur in the absence of a diagnosable mental illness
EEG is likely to show beta rhythm
Such experiences can occur only in the auditory modality
It is a sign of nocturnal epilepsy

correct_answer.text: It can occur in the absence of a diagnosable mental illness

A hypnagogic hallucination is a transient false perception experienced while on the verge of falling asleep. The same phenomenon experienced while waking up is called a hypnopompic hallucination. These may have the characteristics of true or pseudo-hallucinations and are most commonly visual or auditory. While they are sometimes seen in narcolepsy or affective illnesses, they are not indicative of ill health and are frequently reported by healthy people.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 73, 112.

questions.question_text: This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: Mitgehen refers to a form of extreme cooperation in which the patient moves their body in the direction of the slightest pressure on the part of the examiner. For example, the doctor puts his forefinger under the patient's arm and presses gently, after that the arm moves upwards in the direction of the pressure. Once the pressure stops, the arm returns to its former position. Light pressure on the occiput of the patient, who is standing, leads to bending of the neck, flexing of the trunk and, if the pressure continues, the patient may fall forward.

questions.question_text: The most common type of seizure with an aura is
questions.explanation:
Preictal events (auras) in complex partial seizures include autonomic sensations (e.g., fullness in the stomach, blushing, and changes in respiration); cognitive sensations (e.g., déjà vu, jamais vu, forced thinking, dreamy states); affective states (e.g., fear, panic, depression, elation); and classically, automatisms (e.g., lip smacking, rubbing, chewing).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 251.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not a motor symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Cataplexy is a symptom of narcolepsy in which there is sudden loss of muscle tone, leading to collapse. This usually occurs following emotional stress. Recognised motor symptoms of schizophrenia include catatonia, catalepsy, negativism, ambitendency, psychological pillow, mannerism, stereotypy, echopraxia, mitmachen, mitgehen and automatic obedience.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: In formal thought disorder, asyndesis refers to
questions.explanation:
Asyndesis (also known as loosening of associations) is a symptom of formal thought disorder in which there is a lack of meaningful connection between sequential ideas. Cameron (1944), used the term 'asyndesis' to describe the lack of adequate connections or causal links between successive thoughts.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 103, 113.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with Ganser syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 236.
Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1- 22.

questions.question_text: What is the correct term to describe this scenario?
questions.explanation:
One approach to separating ‘normal’ from ‘pathological’ requires that either distress or functional impairment be present in order to make a diagnosis. While DSM requires distress or functional impairment, ICD requires both. Unless there is some evidence of this, it must be considered as normal.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019.pp. 14-15.

questions.question_text: Automatism is a recognised phenomenon seen most commonly in patients with
questions.explanation:
An automatism is a behaviour which is apparently conscious in nature, occurring in the absence of full consciousness (e.g. during a temporal lobe seizure).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 103.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a feature associated with alexithymia?

options.text: Difficulties in differentiating body sensations and emotional states
Difficulties in recognising one's own feelings

questions.explanation:
Patients with alexithymia know very little about their own feelings and, in most instances, are unable to link them with memories, fantasies, or specific situations. Salient features of alexithymia include:
- Difficulty identifying feelings - Difficulty distinguishing between feelings and the bodily sensations of emotional arousal
- Difficulty describing feelings to other people
- Constricted imaginal processes, as evidenced by a paucity of fantasy
- A stimulus-bound, externally-oriented cognitive style
Ref: Goerlich KS. The multifaceted nature of alexithymia–a neuroscientific perspective. Frontiers in psychology. 2018 Aug 29;9:1614.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the commonest cause of stupor in psychiatric units?
questions.explanation:
Stupor is a state of more or less complete loss of activity where there is no reaction to external stimuli. It can be regarded as an extreme form of hypokinesia. Stupor may occur in states of shock, dissociative or conversion disorders, depression, psychosis, catatonia, and organic brain disease. The most common cause of stupor in psychiatric units is depression.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 98.

questions.question_text: A dominating but solitary belief that is neither delusional nor obsessional but influences one's life to a notable extent is called
questions.explanation:
An over-valued idea is a form of abnormal belief that is reasonable and understandable in itself, but which comes to unreasonably dominate the patient’s life. It is a thought that, because of the associated feeling tone, takes precedence over all other ideas and maintains this precedence permanently or for a long period of time. Over-valued ideas tend to be less fixed than delusions and tend to have some degree of basis in reality.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 115.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 48.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a first rank symptom of schizophrenia?

options.text: Voices giving repeated feedback as and when the patient does an act
Voices giving commentary on the patient

questions.explanation:
A command hallucination is an auditory hallucination of a commanding voice, instructing the patient towards a particular action. It is also known as a teleological hallucination and is not a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia. In first rank symptoms, patients may hear voices commenting on what they are doing, discussing it between themselves, or reporting the patient’s own thoughts back to them.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 78-79, 104.

questions.question_text: Circumstantial speech is seen in all EXCEPT
questions.explanation:
Circumstantial thinking is a disorder of the form of thought where irrelevant details and digressions overwhelm the direction of the thought process. This abnormality may be reflected in the resultant speech and can be seen in a number of conditions including mania and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. In contrast, Broca aphasia (also called non-fluent aphasia) is characterised by non-fluent speech and somewhat impaired repetition.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 48.

questions.question_text: Dysmorphophobia is typically a/an
questions.explanation:
Dysmorphophobia is a type of over-valued idea where the patient believes that one aspect of their body is abnormal or conspicuously deformed.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 109.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are the two stages in a delusional perception?

options.text: Recall of abnormal memory and delusional significance

questions.explanation:
A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience. A delusional perception is the attribution of a new meaning, usually in the sense of self-reference, to a normally perceived object. Schneider emphasised the importance of a delusional perception’s ‘two memberedness’, as there is a link from the perceived object to the subject’s perception of this object, and a second link to the new significance of the perception.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 107.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. pp. 48-49.

questions.question_text: Psychomotor retardation is a characteristic feature of
questions.explanation:
Psychomotor retardation is characterised by decreased spontaneous movement and slowness in instigating and completing voluntary movement. It is usually associated with a subjective sense of actions being more of an effort and with subjective retardation of thought. It occurs in moderate to severe depressive illness.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 117.

questions.question_text: Musical hallucinations has been reported in all of the following except
questions.explanation: Hearing loss or deafness is a very important factor associated with musical hallucinations. The hallucinatory experiences are more intense when the surrounding noise is low. Brain imaging studies of patients with musical hallucinations reveal a dysfunctional temporal cortex, especially on the left more than the right hemisphere.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The prominent negative symptoms include affective flattening or blunting, attentional impairment, avolition-apathy (lack of initiative), anhedonia, asociality, alogia (lack of speech output).

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not a first rank symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Thought blocking is not a first-rank symptom. First rank symptoms of schizophrenia are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. First rank symptoms can be categorised as follows:
- Auditory hallucinations (voices heard arguing, thought echo, running commentary)
- Delusions of thought interference (thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting)
- Delusions of control (passivity of affect, passivity of impulse, passivity of volitions, somatic passivity)
- Delusional perception (a primary delusion of any content that is reported by the patient as having arisen following the experience of a normal perception)
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 110.

questions.explanation:
Parapraxis is a faulty act, such as a slip of the tongue or the misplacement of an article. Freud ascribed parapraxes to unconscious motives.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1142.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes a hypnagogic hallucination?

options.text: Hallucinations on waking up from sleep
Hallucinations that occur only in day time sleep
Hallucinations that form a part of dreaming
Hallucinations that induce a sleep-like state

A hypnagogic hallucination is a transient false perception experienced while on the verge of falling asleep. These may have the characteristics of true or pseudo-hallucinations and are most commonly visual or auditory. While they are sometimes seen in narcolepsy or affective illnesses, they are not indicative of ill health and are frequently reported by healthy people.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 73, 112.

questions.question_text: The most appropriate psychopathology described here is
questions.explanation:
Thought withdrawal is the delusion that one’s thoughts are being removed from one’s mind by other people or forces. Schneider gave the description of a man who was experiencing thought withdrawal in the above format.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1144.

questions.question_text: Psychopathology of near death experiences include all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Near-death experiences are often strikingly similar. They often involve an out-of-body experience of viewing one’s own body (autoscopy) and overhearing conversations, feelings of peace, hearing a distant voice, entering a dark tunnel, leaving the body behind, meeting dead loved ones, witnessing beings of light, returning to life to complete unfinished business, and deep sadness on leaving this new dimension. Motor perseveration is not a part of this experience.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 848.

questions.question_text: Echolalia is characterised by

options.text: Automatic repetition of one's own speech
Automatic repetition of the actions of others
Automatic repetition of one's own actions
Virtual absence of movement and speech but preserved consciousness
Automatic repetition of another person's speech

correct_answer.text: Automatic repetition of another person's speech

correct_answers.text: Automatic repetition of another person's speech

questions.explanation:
Echolalia is the repetition of phrases or sentences spoken by others (e.g., the examiner). Echopraxia refers to the automatic repetition of visually perceived actions of others. Akinetic mutism is the virtual absence of movement and speech in the presence of full consciousness.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 109.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation: Reaction times are decreased in response to words preceded by semantically related words ('cat'-'dog') in comparison with words preceded by semantically unrelated words ('bus'-'dog'), this is known as semantic priming effect. "When a concept node is activated by corresponding word stimulus, this activation then spreads through the network to connected nodes, falling off with decreasing relatedness. The degree to which one concept activates another is thus presumably proportional to their relatedness in the semantic network". Large priming effects for indirectly related words (those related only through at least one other concept, such as 'cat' and 'cheese,' mediated by 'mouse') have been observed in schizophrenia patients with thought disorder. This is called indirect priming. [Excerpts from Kiang et al., Am J Psychiatry 2008; 165:74-81]

questions.question_text: The phenomenon of deja vu is

options.text: Inappropriate familiarity to a new place or event
Transient loss of sense of familiarity to a well accustomed place
Inappropriate familiarity with a new thought
Loss of sense of familiarity to a well known person

correct_answer.text: Inappropriate familiarity to a new place or event

correct_answers.text: Inappropriate familiarity to a new place or event

questions.explanation:
Déjà vu is a sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before. It is not strictly a disturbance of memory, but a problem with familiarity of places and events. It comprises the feeling of having experienced a current event in the past, although it has no basis in fact. The converse, jamais vu, is the knowledge that an event has been experienced before but is not presently associated with the appropriate feelings of familiarity. Deja entendu, the feeling of auditory recognition, and deja pense, a new thought recognised as having previously occurred, are related to deja vu, being different only in the modality of experience. These can be experienced by normal subjects as well as among those with temporal lobe epilepsy.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 105.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 69.

questions.question_text: Astasia-abasia has been observed in
questions.explanation:
Astasia-abasia is a gait disturbance that has been seen in conversion disorder. It is a wildly ataxic, staggering gait accompanied by gross, irregular, jerky truncal movements and thrashing and waving arm movements. Patients with the symptoms rarely fall; if they do, they are generally not injured.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 455.

questions.question_text: Which term could be used to describe this psychopathology?
questions.explanation: Outcome fear is a diagnostic feature of panic disorder. The bias in information processing that leads to outcome fear is termed as catastrophic misinterpretation.

questions.question_text: According to Jaspers which of the following is true about primary delusions?

options.text: They are un-understandable in terms of other mental experiences
They have prognostic significance in schizophrenia

correct_answer.text: They are un-understandable in terms of other mental experiences

correct_answers.text: They are un-understandable in terms of other mental experiences

questions.explanation:
Jaspers maintained that primary delusions were typical of un-understandable phenomena, being immediately experienced by the patients as absolutely self-evident like an intuition or a revelation and accompanied by abnormalities in the form such as radical transformation or emergence of thinking. He designated primary delusions as delusion proper, from which secondary delusions evolve via conscious thought processes.
Ref: Hayashi N et al. Delusion progression process from the perspective of patients with psychoses: A descriptive study based on the primary delusion concept of Karl Jaspers. Plos one. 2021 Apr 27;16(4):e0250766.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true?

options.text: He has extrapyramidal rigidity from antipsychotics
He has spasticity due to cerebrovascular pathology

questions.explanation:
Catatonia is characterised by increased resting muscle tone that is not present on active or passive movement (in contrast to the rigidity associated with Parkinson disease and extra-pyramidal side effects).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: All of the following are accepted as neologisms except

options.text: Personal jargon invented to describe the schizophrenic experience
A phrase constructed with incorrect grammar
A new word incorrectly built up with origins clearly understandable
An accepted word used in an unusual way acquiring a new meaning
Completely new word, the derivation of which cannot be understood

correct_answer.text: A phrase constructed with incorrect grammar

correct_answers.text: A phrase constructed with incorrect grammar

questions.explanation:
Neologisms may be new words that are constructed by the patient or ordinary words that are used in a new way. The term ‘neologism’ is usually applied to new word formations produced by individuals with schizophrenia. When an individual with schizophrenia produces a new word, it may be completely new and its derivation cannot be understood; it may be a distortion of another word; or it may be a word that has been incorrectly constructed by the faulty use of the accepted rules of word formation.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 57.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is characterised by patients maintaining unusual postures for long time with no resistance to a passive movement?
questions.explanation:
Mitmachen is a motor symptom of schizophrenia where the patient’s limbs can be moved without resistance to any position. The limbs return to their resting state once the examiner lets go, in contrast with catalepsy (or waxy flexibility) where the limbs remain in their set positions for prolonged periods. Mitgehen is an extreme form of mitmachen where the patient’s limbs can be moved to any position by very slight or fingertip pressure.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 114.

questions.question_text: Overinclusive thinking is tested by using a
questions.explanation:
Abstract attitude is a term introduced by German psychiatrist Kurt Goldstein to denote the ability to use conceptual categories in order to classify things according to their attributes and to think symbolically rather than concretely. Goldstein’s sorting test requires the respondent to sort items into categories according to colour, form, and material. It can be used to test overinclusion.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. pp. 4, 318.

A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation:
In a functional hallucination, an auditory stimulus causes a hallucination, but the stimulus as well as the hallucination is experienced. In other words, the hallucination requires the presence of another real sensation. (For example, a patient with schizophrenia first heard the voice of God as her clock ticked; later she heard voices coming from the running tap and voices coming from the chirruping of the birds.) Patients can distinguish both features from each other and crucially, the hallucination does not occur without the stimulus.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 35.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements regarding deja vu and jamais vu is false?

options.text: Deja vu is associated with inappropriate familiarity
Deja vu may occur in normal individuals
Deja vu can occur in schizophrenia
Jamais vu is the sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before
Deja vu occurs more often in TLE with a right-sided focus

correct_answer.text: Jamais vu is the sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before

correct_answers.text: Jamais vu is the sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before

questions.explanation:
Déjà vu is a sense that events being experienced for the first time have been experienced before. Jamais vu is the sensation that events or situations are unfamiliar, although they have been experienced before. Both déjà vu and jamais vu can be everyday experiences, but also non-specific symptoms of a number of disorders, including temporal lobe epilepsy, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 105, 113.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding pseudo-hallucinations?

options.text: Cannot be seen in normal people
Associated with amnesia for the object

questions.explanation:
A pseudo-hallucination is a false perception that is perceived as occurring as part of one’s internal experience, not as part of the external world. It may be described as having an ‘as if’ quality or as being seen with the mind’s eye. Pseudo-hallucinations are a type of mental image that, although clear and vivid, lack the substantiality of perceptions. Pseudo-hallucinations are seen in full consciousness, known to be not real perceptions, and are located not in objective space but in subjective space (for example, inside the head). Like true hallucinations, they are involuntary. Pseudo-hallucinations can occur in all modalities of sensation and are described in psychotic, organic, and drug-induced conditions, as well as occasionally in ‘normal’ individuals. (The hallucinations of deceased spouses commonly described by widows and widowers may have a form of a pseudo-hallucination.)
Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 116, 236.
Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1- 22.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 28.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is NOT an elementary hallucination?

options.text: Unstructured flakes of images in a delirious patient

questions.explanation:
Hallucinations may be elementary and unformed, and experienced as simple noises, bells, or undifferentiated whispers. Elemental hallucinations are of very simple form (e.g. flashes of light or unstructured noises such as clicks and bangs). Elementary auditory hallucinations can occur in organic states and schizophrenia.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 30.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 109.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a catatonic sign?
questions.explanation:
Catatonia is a syndrome of primarily psychomotor disturbances characterised by the occurrence of several different symptoms including stupor; catalepsy/waxy flexibility/flexibilitas cerea; mutism; negativism; posturing; mannerisms; stereotypies; psychomotor agitation; grimacing; echolalia; echopraxia; ambitendency (alternating mixture of automatic obedience and negativism).
Essential tremor (6-12Hz) occurs at rest, with action and postural. It is most noticeable symmetrically in the upper limbs. It is not a catatonic sign.
Ref: Gaebel W et al. Changes from ICD-10 to ICD-11 and future directions in psychiatric classification. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2020 Mar;22(1):7.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 132.

questions.question_text: Obsessional slowness is common in which of the following type of obsessions?
questions.explanation: An obsessive need for symmetry and exactness and a compulsion to order and arrange often results in slowness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is least likely to be true in this case?

options.text: This phenomenon can occur due to anticholinergic toxicity
This phenomenon is reported in delirium tremens
The perception has occurred without appropriate stimulus
This phenomenon is associated with organic disorders of the brain
Presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder than an organic mental illness

correct_answer.text: Presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder than an organic mental illness

correct_answers.text: Presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder than an organic mental illness

questions.explanation:
An hallucination is an internal percept without a corresponding external object. Auditory hallucinations, particularly of voices, are characteristic of schizophrenic illness, whjle visual hallucinations are characteristic of organic states. All varieties of visual hallucinations are found in organic states, but small animals and insects are most often hallucinated in delirium.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 112.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 32.

questions.question_text: Eidetic imagery is best classified as a
questions.explanation:
Eidetic imagery is a particular type of exceptionally vivid visual memory. It is not a hallucination. It is more common in children than adults.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 109.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about this?

options.text: It is a type of hallucination

questions.explanation: Eidetic images represent visual memories of almost hallucinatory vividness that are found in disorders due to substance misuse, especially hallucinogenic agents such as LSD and mescaline. It is seen more commonly in children and those involved in group religious practices.

questions.question_text: Schnauzkrampf is associated with
questions.explanation:
The muscle tension in catatonic stupor (most commonly seen in schizophrenia) is usually increased in the muscles of the forehead and the masseters. The lips may be thrust forward in a tubular manner known as ‘snout spasm’ (Schnauzkrampf). Although this is obviously a disorder of expression, it is best regarded as a stereotyped posture.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019.pp. 88, 98.

questions.question_text: Of various thought disorders classified by Andreasen, which of the following is more common in schizophrenia than mania?
questions.explanation:
Nancy Andreasen created a scale in which the classic formal thought disorders are subdivided into three groups:
- Communication disturbances: when the speaker does not meet the necessary requirements for the listener’s understanding (poverty of content of speech, pressure of speech, distractible speech, tangentiality, derailment, stilted speech, echolalia, self-reference, circumstantiality, loss of goal, perseveration, and blocking)
- Language disturbances: when the speaker violates the semantic and syntactic conventions (incoherence, clang association, neologisms, use of word approximations)
- Thought disturbances: when only thinking alone seems affected (poverty of thought and illogically aberrant inferential processes)
Andreasen demonstrated that these psychopathological findings were not specific to schizophrenia and were also common in other mental disorders (e.g. mania). Of those listed, derailment (synonymous with loose associations - a symptom of schizophrenic thought disorder in which there is a total break in the chain of association between the meaning of thoughts) is more common in schizophrenia than mania.
Ref: Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108.

questions.question_text: Choose one of the following statements that is true about autochthonous delusions.

options.text: Autochthonous delusion is a type of secondary delusion
Autochthonous delusions and wahneinfall are equivalent terms
Autochthonous delusions may give rise to secondary delusions
Retrospective delusions are the same as autochthonous delusions

correct_answer.text: Autochthonous delusions may give rise to secondary delusions

correct_answers.text: Autochthonous delusions may give rise to secondary delusions

questions.explanation:
An autochthonous delusion is a primary delusion which appears to arise fully formed in the patient’s mind without explanation. Primary delusions are the direct result of psychopathology, while secondary delusions can be understood as having arisen in response to other primary psychiatric conditions. If the patient is asked to recall the point when they became aware of the delusion and its significance to them, they may report that it arose ‘out of the blue’, which is an autochthonous delusion. Primary delusions such as autochthonous delusions may give rise to many secondary delusions that get tightly systematised later. For example, a patient who suddenly gets an autochthonous idea that Martians are invading his office may then start connecting normal behaviours of his colleagues to Martians and may form a systematised belief complex involving cameras, alien sign languages, UFOs etc.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 103, 106.

A delusional perception is a primary delusion of any content that is reported by the patient as having arisen following the experience of a normal perception. If the patient is asked to recall the point when they became aware of the delusion and its significance to them, they will report that the delusional perception arose on seeing a normal percept (the percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience). Delusional perception is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Reduced symbolic thinking is a feature of
questions.explanation:
Patients with alexithymia know very little about their own feelings and, in most instances, are unable to link them with memories, fantasies, or specific situations. Salient features of alexithymia include:
- Difficulty identifying feelings
- Difficulty distinguishing between feelings and the bodily sensations of emotional arousal
- Difficulty describing feelings to other people
- Constricted imaginal processes, as evidenced by a paucity of fantasy
- A stimulus-bound, externally-oriented cognitive style

questions.explanation:
A pseudo-hallucination is a false perception that is perceived as occurring as part of one’s internal experience, not as part of the external world. It may be described as having an ‘as if’ quality or as being seen with the mind’s eye. Pseudo-hallucinations are a type of mental image that, although clear and vivid, lack the substantiality of perceptions. Pseudo-hallucinations are seen in full consciousness, known to be not real perceptions, and are located not in objective space but in subjective space (for example, inside the head). Like true hallucinations, they are involuntary. Pseudo-hallucinations can occur in all modalities of sensation and are described in psychotic, organic, and drug-induced conditions, as well as occasionally in ‘normal’ individuals. (The hallucinations of deceased spouses commonly described by widows and widowers may have a form of a pseudo-hallucination.)
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 116.

An individual develops a delusion similar to another individual who already has an established delusion; usually the two individuals have a close relationship (often sisters). In DSM-5, this is termed as Shared Psychotic Disorder.
Note: Folie a trios - madness shared by three. Folie a quatre - madness shared by four. Folie a famille - madness shared by the family. Folie a plusieurs - madness shared by many.

questions.question_text: Which of the following syndromes and delusional types are not correctly associated?

options.text: Morbid jealousy - delusions of marital infidelity
De Clerambault syndrome - delusions of love
Couvade syndrome - delusion of pregnancy in postpartum mothers

correct_answer.text: Couvade syndrome - delusion of pregnancy in postpartum mothers

questions.explanation:
Othello syndrome (morbid jealousy): a monosymptomatic delusional disorder where the core delusion has the content of delusional jealousy
De Clerambault syndrome: a form of delusion of love in which the patient, usually female, believes that another, higher-status individual is in love with them
Cotard syndrome: a presentation of psychotic depressive illness seen particularly in elderly people where there is a combination of severely depressed mood with nihilistic delusions and/or hypochondriacal delusions
Ekbom syndrome: a monosymptomatic delusional disorder where the core delusion is a delusion of infestation
Couvade syndrome: a conversion symptom seen in partners of expectant mothers during their pregnancy; symptoms vary, but mimic pregnancy symptoms; NOT delusional in nature – the affected individual does not believe that they are pregnant

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a type of abnormal induced movement?
questions.explanation:
Some abnormal induced movements can be regarded as the result of undue compliance on the part of the patient, while others may be interpreted as indicating rejection of the environment. For example, in automatic obedience the patient carries out every instruction regardless of the consequence. While stereotypy is a spontaneous abnormal movement, perseveration is an induced movement because it is a senseless repetition of a goal-directed action that has already served its purpose.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. pp. 92-93.

questions.question_text: La belle indifference is typically seen in
questions.explanation:
(La) belle indifference is a surprising lack of concern for, or denial of, apparently severe functional disability. It is part of classical descriptions of hysteria and continues to be associated with operational descriptions of conversion disorder. It is also seen in medical illnesses (e.g. following a stroke) and is a rare and non-specific symptom of no diagnostic value.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 103.

questions.question_text: In pure word blindness which of the following is true?
questions.explanation:
Pure word blindness (also known as ‘pure alexia’, ‘alexia without agraphia’, and ‘agnostic alexia’) is characterised by various degrees of impaired word reading with no deficits in the production or comprehension of oral language, and a preserved ability to write spontaneously or on dictation.
Ref: Martinaud O. Visual agnosia and focal brain injury. Revue neurologique. 2017 Jul 1;173(7-8):451-60.

questions.question_text: This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: Lilliputian hallucinations are a type of visual hallucination in which the subject sees miniature people or animals. They are associated with organic states, particularly delirium tremens.

questions.question_text: In logoclonia, the subject keeps repeating which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Logoclonia refers to meaningless repetition of a syllable, especially an end syllable of a word. It was first reported among individuals with dementia by Kraepelin in 1910 who described is as a severe linguistic dysfunction observed in the advanced stages of early-onset Alzheimer disease. Logoclonia has been described by several neurologists since then and has often been linked to Alzheimer disease. Palilalia and stuttering have disorders that are similar to those of logoclonia and have been associated with Parkinson disease and progressive supranuclear palsy. Palilalia, however, refers to the repetition of an entire word, but not a syllable. Stuttering is the involuntary disruption or blocking of speech with sound repetition, especially the initial consonants of a word, and, unlike logoclonia, stuttering is accompanied by tense and effortful utterance.
Ref: Nakagawa Y et al. Logoclonia might be a Characteristic of Logopenic Variant Primary Progressive Aphasia at an Advanced Stage: Potential Mechanisms Underlying Logoclonia. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2019 Jan 1;70(2):515-24.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning depersonalisation?

options.text: It is experienced as an unpleasant state
The subject feels that the world around him is unreal
Multiple personalities emerge during the experience
It is associated with approximate answers
The subject cannot recall events later

correct_answer.text: It is experienced as an unpleasant state

correct_answers.text: It is experienced as an unpleasant state

questions.explanation:
Depersonalisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if they have become ‘unreal’. It is a feeling that one is not oneself or that something has changed. Depersonalisation is a non-specific symptom occurring in many psychiatric disorders, as well as in ‘normal’ people.
Derealisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if the world has become unreal. It is a feeling that one’s environment has changed in some strange way that is difficult to describe. Like depersonalisation, derealisation is also a non-specific symptom of a number of disorders.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 108.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10.

questions.question_text: Flashback phenomenon is commonly reported after ingesting which of the following substances?
questions.explanation:
Long after ingesting a hallucinogen, a person can experience a flashback of hallucinogenic symptoms. Flashbacks are spontaneous, transitory recurrences of the substance-induced experience. Most flashbacks are episodes of visual distortion, geometric hallucinations, hallucinations of sounds or voices, false perceptions of movement in peripheral fields, flashes of colour, trails of images from moving objects, positive afterimages and halos, macropsia, micropsia, time expansion, physical symptoms, or relived intense emotion.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 322-323.

questions.question_text: Coenesthetic hallucinations are a type of
questions.explanation:
Coenesthesia is an awareness of one’s own body. Somatic hallucinations with peculiar visceral, bodily, or tactile perceptions in the absence of sensorial input are coenesthetic hallucinations. Such hallucinations of pain and deep sensations are ‘visceral’ hallucinations. Some patients may complain of twisting and tearing pains. These may be very bizarre when the patient complains that their organs are being torn out or the flesh ripped away from the body.
Ref: Nasser A et al. A case of coenesthetic hallucinations treated with low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. Brain Stimulation: Basic, Translational, and Clinical Research in Neuromodulation. 2017 Jul 1;10(4):845-6.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 34.

questions.question_text: Overvalued ideas are NOT noted in the core symptoms of which one of the following disorder?
questions.explanation: PTSD is an anxiety disorder; overvalued ideas are not described in the diagnostic criteria of PTSD

questions.question_text: One-way amnesia is associated with
questions.explanation: In multiple personality disorder, one-way amnesia is reported. One-way amnesia refers to the phenomenon where in the personality A knows B's existence, while B is not aware of A's life.
