questions.explanation: In automatic obedience the patient carries out every instruction regardless of the consequence. To demonstrate this, Emil Kraepelin would ask the patient to put out their tongue and he would prick it with a pin; patients with automatic obedience continued to put their tongue out when asked to, although every time they did so their tongue was pricked

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false with regard to pseudohallucinations?

options.text: Patient may have insight about the absence of reality
May occur in a subjective space  (e.g. within the head)
Patient does not usually search for the bearer of the voice

questions.explanation:
Explanations:
Pseudo-hallucinations are a type of mental image that, although clear and vivid, lack the substantiality of perceptions. They are experienced in full consciousness, known to be not real perceptions, and are located not in objective space but subjective space (for example, inside the head). Pseudo-hallucinations can occur in all modalities of sensation and are described in psychotic, organic, and drug-induced conditions, as well as occasionally in ‘normal’ individuals.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 28.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 116.

questions.question_text: Auditory hallucinations with clear consciousness are least likely to be due to
questions.explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis, any functional psychiatric disorder, and early dementia can cause auditory hallucinations with clear consciousness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a thought disorder where figure-ground differentiation apparently fails?
questions.explanation: Circumstantiality occurs when thinking proceeds slowly with many unnecessary and trivial details, but finally the point is reached. The goal of thinking is never completely lost and thinking proceeds towards it by an intricate and convoluted path, and is often due to the loss of figure-ground differentiation in the thought process (From Fish's Psychopathology. 3rd ed).

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
A compulsion is a behaviour or action that is recognised by the patient as unnecessary and purposeless, but that they cannot resist performing repeatedly. It is an obsessional motor act. Compulsive acts may not be preceded by an identifiable obsession, especially in disorders other than OCD such as autism, dementia, Tourette, etc. where they can be seen without preceding obsessions.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 104.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition.
2019. p. 46.

questions.question_text: What is the psychopathology seen in this case?
questions.explanation:
Emotionalism (or emotional incontinence) is characterised by an increase in emotional behaviour (crying or, less commonly, laughing) following minimal provoking stimuli. Patients may persistently cry or laugh in unexpected situations.
Ref: Bowen A et al. Royal College of Physicians 2016 National clinical guideline for stroke. RCP.

questions.question_text: This can be described as which of the following symptoms?
questions.explanation:
A delusional memory is a primary delusion that is recalled as arising as a result of a memory.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 106.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about first rank symptoms of schizophrenia is NOT true?

options.text: They are also seen in organic psychoses
These are a group of symptoms which are useful in the diagnosis of schizophrenia
They are also seen in affective psychoses
They are neither pathognomonic nor specific to schizophrenia

questions.explanation:
First rank symptoms of schizophrenia are a group of symptoms that have special significance in the diagnosis of schizophrenia. They are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. However, there is no symptom that is pathognomonic of schizophrenia. First rank symptoms can all be reported in other conditions (e.g. organic psychoses, manic illnesses). They do not give a guide to severity or prognosis of illness, and they may not occur at all in a patient who undoubtedly has schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 78.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a type of catatonic phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Catatonia is a syndrome of primarily psychomotor disturbances characterised by the occurrence of several different symptoms including stupor; catalepsy/waxy flexibility/flexibilitas cerea; mutism; negativism; posturing; mannerisms; stereotypies; psychomotor agitation; grimacing; echolalia; echopraxia; ambitendency (alternating mixture of automatic obedience and negativism).
Waxy flexibility (also known as catalepsy or flexibilitas cerea) is a rare motor symptom in which the patient’s limbs can be passively moved to any posture, which will then be held for a prolonged period of time.
Ref: Gaebel W et al. Changes from ICD-10 to ICD-11 and future directions in psychiatric classification. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2020 Mar;22(1):7.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the above sign?
questions.explanation: In catatonia the lips may be thrust forward in a tubular manner known as 'snout spasm' (or schnauzkrampf) and although this is obviously a disorder of expression it is best regarded as a stereotyped posture.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about first rank symptoms of schizophrenia?

options.text: They are essential for diagnosing schizophrenia
They are not seen in other psychiatric disorders
They emphasize on content rather than form

questions.explanation:
First rank symptoms (FRS) of schizophrenia are a group of symptoms that have special significance in the diagnosis of schizophrenia. They are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. However, there is no symptom that is pathognomonic of schizophrenia. FRS can all be reported in other conditions (e.g. organic psychoses, manic illnesses). They do not give a guide to severity or prognosis of illness, and they may not occur at all in a patient who undoubtedly has schizophrenia. The original psychoanalytic interpretation of FRS is that the boundary between the ego and the surrounding world breaks down, leading to thought and volition being alienated.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 78.

options.text: It cannot occur unless she is completely blind in at least one eye
The rabbit will not disappear on sleeping
The objects seen are usually static

questions.explanation:
Charles Bonnet syndrome (phantom visual images) is a condition in which complex visual hallucinations occur in the absence of any psychopathology and in clear consciousness. It is associated with either central or peripheral reduction in vision. The images may be static or in motion. They may be enjoyable or distressing. Patients may retain insight.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. pp. 29, 124.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a term used to describe the phenomenon of hearing one's own thoughts aloud?
questions.explanation:
Gedankenlautwerden (also known as ‘thought echo’ or ‘echo de la pensee’) is the experience of an auditory hallucination in which the content is the individual’s current thoughts. It is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 118.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a type of primary delusion?
questions.explanation: The 4 types of primary delusions include delusional mood, delusional perception, delusional memory and autochthonous delusions

questions.question_text: Which of the following cannot be considered as a component of descriptive psychopathology?
questions.explanation:
Descriptive psychopathology includes close observation of the patient’s behaviour and empathic exploration of their subjective experience. The latter is called phenomenology. Defence mechanisms are best described under psychodynamic (explanatory) psychopathology.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 100.

questions.question_text: This is best described as
questions.explanation:
Thought withdrawal is the delusion that one’s thoughts are being removed from one’s mind by other people or forces.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1144.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes paraschemazia?

options.text: Inappropriate familiarity in a new place
Loss of emotional control following brain injury

questions.explanation:
Paraschemazia or distortion of body image is described as a feeling that parts of the body are distorted or twisted or separated from the rest of the body. This can occur in association with hallucinogenic use, with an epileptic aura, and with migraine on rare occasions.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019.p. 39.

questions.question_text: Retardation of thinking seen in depressive disorder is appropriately classified as which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
With inhibition or slowing of thinking in depression, the train of thought is slowed down and the number of ideas and mental images that present themselves is decreased. This is a disturbance in the stream of thought.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 44.

questions.question_text: Inability to verbalize one's strong emotions is termed as
questions.explanation:
Alexithymia is the inability to describe one’s subjective emotional experiences verbally. It may be a personality characteristic but is also associated with somatisation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 102.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurological disturbances closely mimic schizophrenic speech disturbance?
questions.explanation:
Jargon aphasia is a form of fluent aphasia characterised by a copious flow of unintelligible speech. Jargon-aphasic speech may be subdivided into semantic jargon, in which ordinary words are strung together to form unintelligible utterances, and phonemic jargon involving neologisms. A neologism is a made-up word or normal word used in an idiosyncratic way. Neologisms may be found in schizophrenic speech.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 396.

questions.explanation:
Flattening of affect is the diminution of the normal range of emotional experience and is a negative symptom of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to be seen in an 18-year-old girl with hysterical aphonia?

options.text: Patient loses ability to speak aloud but whispers

correct_answer.text: Patient loses ability to speak aloud but whispers

correct_answers.text: Patient loses ability to speak aloud but whispers

questions.explanation:
Dysarthria: There is difficulty in articulation, which occurs in lesions of the brain stem, schizophrenia and cerebellar disorder.
Dysphonia: Impairment of ability to vocalize with some hoarseness of voice, which occurs in the paralysis of the 9th cranial nerve and disease of vocal cords.
Aphonia: Patient loses ability to vocalise and whispers, occurs in conversion disorders. Aphonia is defined as the absence of vocalization or phonation and differs from mutism, which is the absence of speech. Hysterical aphonia is characterized by a normal whisper and cough. Examination with a laryngoscope reveals normal vocal cord movement with respiration.
